common_name: Jethro Tull Coreopsis (Fringed Spoon-Petaled Threadleaf Coreopsis)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Jethro Tull is a threadleaf coreopsis cultivar with distinctive fluted, spoon-shaped gold petals that give the flowers a fringed, textured look.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; threadleaf coreopsis thrives on soil too poor and dry for many other perennials. Jethro Tull produces bright golden-yellow flowers with distinctively fluted, spoon-shaped petals that curl slightly along their length, giving each bloom a fringed, three-dimensional texture unlike the flatter petals of most other coreopsis cultivars, held above fine, airy, thread-like foliage. It flowers heavily over a long summer season and tolerates heat and drought exceptionally well once established, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for the front of a sunny border or a mass planting. Shear the plant back by about a third after the first flush fades to encourage a fuller rebloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: John Fanick Phlox (Heat-and-Humidity-Tolerant San Antonio Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation; John Fanick, selected in San Antonio, Texas, is noted for exceptional heat and humidity tolerance and a long bloom season.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade with good air circulation to help minimize powdery mildew, the primary phlox disease in humid climates. John Fanick was selected in San Antonio, Texas specifically for its outstanding tolerance of extreme summer heat and humidity, conditions that cause many other tall garden phlox cultivars to decline or succumb to mildew, making it one of the most dependable phlox choices for Gulf South and Texas gardens. It bears soft pink flowers with a darker pink eye in a long bloom season that stretches from early summer well into fall, drawing butterflies and hummingbirds throughout. Deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued bloom, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and airflow.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Dark Towers, a Plant Select introduction, is grown as much for its dark maroon-bronze foliage as for its pale pink tubular flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, since penstemon is prone to crown rot in wet, heavy soil. Dark Towers, a Plant Select introduction, pairs tall spikes of pale pink, tubular flowers with striking dark maroon-bronze foliage that holds its color through the growing season, giving the plant strong ornamental value even between bloom flushes. It attracts hummingbirds and bees while in flower and tolerates heat and drought well once established, needing minimal supplemental water beyond the establishment period. Deadhead spent flower spikes to encourage additional bloom, and avoid overly rich soil or excess fertilizer, which produces weak, floppy growth in penstemon.
sources: Plant Select — Colorado State University / Denver Botanic Gardens

common_name: Purple Smoke Baptisia (Smoky Lavender-Purple False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade; Purple Smoke, a North Carolina Botanical Garden hybrid, bears smoky lavender-purple flower spikes over blue-gray foliage and, once established, needs almost no maintenance.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents being moved once established. Purple Smoke, a hybrid developed at the North Carolina Botanical Garden, bears tall spikes of smoky, charcoal-tinged lavender-purple pea-like flowers held above handsome blue-gray foliage in late spring, followed by dark seedpods that add fall and winter interest and make a distinctive dried arrangement material. Like other Baptisia it is extremely long-lived, drought-tolerant, and essentially maintenance-free once established, functioning almost like a small flowering shrub in the perennial border. Avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants; instead, simply cut the whole plant back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted, and let it develop into a substantial, long-term specimen.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Floristan Liatris (Classic Tall Gayfeather for Cut Flowers and Pollinators)

planting.note: Plant corms in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Floristan is a classic, widely grown gayfeather cultivar bred for uniform, tall flower spikes prized in both pollinator gardens and the cut-flower trade.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Floristan is a classic, long-cultivated selection of native gayfeather bred for tall, uniform, densely packed spikes of fuzzy violet-purple flowers (a white-flowered 'Floristan White' counterpart is also available) that open from the top down, unusual among spike-flowering perennials, making a striking vertical accent in the border. Its reliable, uniform habit has made it a mainstay of the commercial cut-flower trade as well as home gardens, and the flowers are a strong draw for butterflies, bees, and other pollinators through their summer bloom season. Cut spent flower spikes for indoor arrangements or deadhead to tidy the plant, and divide congested clumps of corms every few years in spring or fall to maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Black Adder Agastache (Deep Blue-Violet Long-Blooming Hyssop)

planting.note: Plant transplants in spring in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; Black Adder is a hybrid agastache bred for deep, near-black flower buds opening to rich blue-violet blooms over an unusually long season.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; good drainage is essential, especially through humid summers, since agastache is prone to root and crown rot in soggy soil. Black Adder is a hybrid agastache producing tall, dense spikes of deep purple-black buds that open to rich blue-violet flowers over a long season from summer well into fall, making it one of the showiest and longest-blooming agastache cultivars available. Its aromatic, anise-scented foliage and abundant nectar-rich flowers make it a strong magnet for bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds throughout its extended bloom period. Deadhead spent spikes to encourage continued flowering, and avoid overwatering or heavy fertilization, which can shorten the plant's lifespan and reduce winter hardiness.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes
